headline: Navdeep Bains Wins Ontario Liberal Leadership on Final Ballot, 50.3 to 49.7
subheadline: The former federal industry minister from Mississauga beat MPP Lee Fairclough by less than a point after a nine-month race, and now has to rebuild a party that holds 14 seats.
body:
• Navdeep Bains, 49, was elected leader of the Ontario Liberal Party on November 21, 2026, beating Etobicoke-Lakeshore MPP Lee Fairclough 50.3 per cent to 49.7 per cent on the third and final ballot.
  • Bains is a former federal minister of innovation, science and industry (2015–2021) and a five-time MP for Mississauga and Brampton ridings; CBC News reports he is the first visible minority to lead the Ontario Liberal Party.
  • He inherits a party with 14 seats in the legislature and no seat of his own: he says he will run for one, but will not ask a sitting MPP to step aside, and the next provincial election need not be held until 2030.
  • About 20,510 party members voted in the contest, and the party says turnout rose 15 per cent on the previous leadership race.

Navdeep Bains is the new leader of the Ontario Liberal Party. The former federal cabinet minister won the party's leadership election on the third ballot at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre on Saturday, November 21, edging provincial caucus member Lee Fairclough by less than one percentage point — 50.3 per cent to 49.7 per cent — in front of a crowd of more than 1,000 Liberals, according to CBC News reporting of the result.

The count was close at every stage. On the weighted points system the party uses — 13,255 points in total, with 6,627.5 needed to win — Bains led the first count with 5,848.21 points (44.09 per cent) to Fairclough's 4,470.05 (33.70 per cent), with Stephanie Bowman on 1,703.37 and Dylan Marando on 1,233.37. After Marando and then Bowman were eliminated and their supporters' preferences redistributed, Bains finished with 6,666.32 points to Fairclough's 6,588.68. Party members voted from November 9 to 20, and the Ontario Liberal Party said turnout was up 15 per cent on the previous race.

"This may be the end of a leadership race, ladies and gentlemen, but this is just the beginning of our campaign to replace Doug Ford and the Conservative Party of Ontario."

— Navdeep Bains, after the result was announced

A familiar face from the Trudeau years

Bains, 49, is a Mississauga resident who represented Mississauga and Brampton ridings in Ottawa for 13 years across two spells — Mississauga—Brampton South from 2004 to 2011 and Mississauga—Malton from 2015 to 2021. In Justin Trudeau's government he served as minister of innovation, science and industry from 2015 to 2021. He left a senior role as chief corporate affairs officer at Rogers Communications earlier this spring to return to politics, CBC reported. His campaign, run under the slogan "Let's Lead Again," framed an "Ontario Deal" around regional economic development, job creation and housing access.

https://www.instagram.com/p/Df-XbZFsOgh/

In his victory speech, Bains cast the Liberals as "the party of jobs and growth and economic prosperity," pointed to past Liberal governments' record — full-day kindergarten, smaller class sizes and the creation of the Greenbelt — and promised to reverse the Ford government's changes to the Ontario Student Assistance Program: "We're going to reverse OSAP, ASAP." Premier Doug Ford congratulated him on X, writing that Ontario families are counting on both sides "to work collaboratively and put province over party so we can stand up to tariffs, protect workers and make life more affordable."

The rebuild he inherits

The scale of the task is the story behind the result. The Ontario Liberals governed from 2003 to 2018, then fell to seven seats and lost official party status in 2018 — their worst result since Confederation. They recovered to 14 seats and official status in the 2025 election, but Bains is the third consecutive leader chosen without a seat in the legislature, after Steven Del Duca and Bonnie Crombie. Crombie won only 57 per cent support in a leadership review in September 2025 and resigned in January 2026; John Fraser served as interim leader until this vote.

Bains told reporters he will seek a seat — "I'll definitely be running, and the determination around the exact location will be made at the appropriate time" — but said he would not ask any of the party's 14 MPPs to resign to make room. CBC's analysis noted that party insiders see him as a strong organizer and fundraiser, the skills a rebuild requires, while Progressive Conservative minister Graham McGregor, observing the event, previewed the attack line to come: Bains's years as one of Trudeau's most prominent ministers in Peel Region.

What happens next

Bains now has to build a team and a platform against a Progressive Conservative government that has won three consecutive majorities, with the next election not required until 2030. For Ontario's large South Asian communities — Bains represented two of the most heavily South Asian ridings in Canada during his federal career — his win puts one of their own at the head of a major provincial party for the first time. Whether that translates into seats will be decided in the by-elections and, eventually, the general election he has promised to contest himself.

key_takeaways: Navdeep Bains elected Ontario Liberal leader with 50.3% of the vote.
He is the first visible minority to lead the Ontario Liberal Party.
Bains plans to run for a seat in the legislature.
Party membership turnout increased by 15% compared to the last leadership race.
Bains aims to rebuild the party after significant electoral losses.
